title: The farmer at Kartarpur
hookLine: after the travels he settles by the Ravi, farms the land, and the first Sikh community gathers around him

lines: NOT A PALACE. NOT A CAVE.
cards: You'd expect a different ending. A man walks for years. He's argued with priests, sung for kings and robbers, met yogis in the snow, been taken prisoner by an army.
By now people far beyond his village know his songs. So where does a man like that end up? In a palace?
A great temple? A cave on a mountain? None of those.
He goes to the banks of the river Ravi, in the Punjab, takes off his traveler's clothes, and picks up a plow.

teach.b: The town was called Kartarpur. Kartar means the Creator, and pur means town: the Creator's town. Tradition says Nanak founded it himself, and lived there for the rest of his life.
What he did there is the whole point.
He farmed his own fields. His wife and sons lived with him. And a community gathered around him: farmers, traders, people of every caste, Hindus and Muslims.
Bhai Gurdas, the Sikh poet, describes the rhythm of the place.

teach.h: HYMNS AT DAWN, WORK, HYMNS AT DUSK.
teach.b: In the early morning, before work, the Japji, the long hymn that opens the scripture. In the evening, more singing. In between, a day's honest labor.
And a common kitchen, where everyone ate together. Every idea from the travels, turned into an ordinary Tuesday. Kirat, honest work, like Lalo the carpenter.
Sharing, in the kitchen. Remembering God, morning and evening. In the world, unstained, like the lotus.
Nanak didn't just tell the yogis to live in the world. He came home and showed them how.
That's why Sikhs often speak of Kartarpur as the first Sikh community, a pattern gurdwaras still echo.
And the place is still there. Kartarpur is now in Pakistan, just across the border from India, and for a long time Sikhs in India could only look at it from the border.
In recent years a corridor opened so Indian pilgrims could cross and visit, though it has been closed at times since.

how: Sikhs honor Kartarpur, now in Pakistan, as the place where Guru Nanak lived out the pattern of work, worship and sharing that gurdwaras follow today; the Kartarpur Corridor has let pilgrims from India visit Gurdwara Darbar Sahib there when it is open.

games.q: you're Nanak. years of travel are done, and people know your songs. where do you spend the rest of your life?
o: in a grand temple built for you.
on a farm by the river, working the land.
games.why: he founded Kartarpur and farmed his own fields, and a community of every caste and faith gathered around him.

practice: Work with your hands for five minutes, and if you can, start now while the bell runs: water a plant, knead dough, scrub a pan, fix a hinge. No phone, no podcast; feel the weight of it, the texture.
Just the work, the way a farmer at Kartarpur might have done it between a morning hymn and an evening one.

wordCard.voice: Kartarpur. The Creator's town, by the river Ravi, where Guru Nanak farmed and the first Sikh community gathered. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Kartarpur, the Creator's town; kartar, the Creator, is a name for God across the Sikh hymns.
